newsitem.title: INDIA: India said inching towards airline plan.
newsitem.headline: India said inching towards airline plan.

text.p: India is inching towards approval of a landmark proposal from the Tata group to set up a domestic airline in partnership with Singapore Airlines, a senior government official said on Monday.
"It is likely to come through," the official, who is close to negotiations, said of the Tatas' $600 million plan which has divided India's ruling coalition.
"Something is happening. That's all I can say," said the official, who asked not to be identified. He was referring to a debate within the government on differences on the proposal.
The Tata proposal, presented in 1995, has become a test case for foreign investors eyeing India under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.

Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim has publicly opposed the proposed Tata Airline, in which Singapore Airlines and the Tatas would hold 40 percent each. The rest of the shareholding is proposed to be sold to Indian institutional investors.
Industry Minister Murasoli Maran, however, supports the Tata-SIA proposal.
Two weeks ago, India approved an aviation policy that allowed foreign stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines, but specifically barred foreign airlines from acquiring stakes.
The Tata-SIA plan was sent back to Ibrahim's ministry for reconsideration.
Ibrahim has said India cannot allow Singapore Airlines to take a stake in a domestic airline because Singapore does not allow foreign stakes of more than five percent in its own airlines.

Officials said last week the government was expected to rethink the policy to consider direct stakes for foreign airlines. The Economic Times newspaper said on Monday that the cabinet would discuss the matter on Tuesday.
No official confirmation was available on the meeting.

The Times of India newspaper quoted a senior Civil Aviation Ministry official as saying that the ministry was likely to approve the Tata-Singapore Airlines proposal, but with some changes in its proposed terms.
The Tatas plan to start the new airline with 19 aircraft. The Times of India quoted the unnamed official as saying the Tatas would have to start off with fewer aircraft.
"They will have come in with much fewer aircraft," he said.

"In future, if they want to induct more aircraft, they would have to get the clearance on a case-to-case basis from the Aircraft Acquisition Committee. This is the way every private airline operates in India," he said.

The Tatas, India's largest private sector group in terms of sales, say they are seeking Singapore Airlines' expertise in high-quality service, safety standards, economic efficiency and staff training.
The Tatas, who pioneered India's aviation industry before airline nationalisation in 1953, had group sales in excess of 265 billion rupees ($7.5 billion) in 1995/96 (April-March).
The group owned India's main airline before independence from British rule in 1947. Private airlines were revived after India started economic reforms in 1991. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
